## B3_2: Extending models — SEIR, demography & time-varying parameters {.title-slide}

Coding compartmental models with R and odin

[Session book: notes, exercises and solutions](../index.html){style="font-size: 0.55em;"}

```{r}
#| include: false
library(odin)
t <- seq(0, 150, by = 1)
```

## Recap of lecture 1

- odin models are equations, not code — compiled to C once, then fast to
  run
- `odin::odin({...})` returns a generator; `generator$new(pars...)`
  creates an instance; `$run(t)` integrates it
- Scenarios are repeated `$new()` calls with different parameters
- Add a `deriv()` line for derived quantities (e.g. cumulative incidence)

Today: grow the SIR skeleton — latent periods, population dynamics and
parameters that change over time.

## Adding a latent period: SEIR

For many infections people are exposed but not yet infectious — a latent
period. Add an Exposed compartment $E$; exposed people become infectious
at rate $\sigma$ (so $1/\sigma$ is the mean latent period):

$$
\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta SI, \quad
\frac{dE}{dt} = \beta SI - \sigma E, \quad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \sigma E - \gamma I, \quad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I
$$

## SEIR in odin

In odin this means one more compartment and re-routing the flows:

```{r}
seir_generator <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I
  deriv(E) <- beta * S * I - sigma * E
  deriv(I) <- sigma * E - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(E) <- 0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N0    <- user(1000)
  I0    <- user(1)
  beta  <- user(2e-4)  # R0 = beta * N / gamma = 2
  gamma <- user(0.1)   # infectious period 10 days
  sigma <- user(0.25)  # latent period 4 days
})
```

## SEIR dynamics

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
y_seir <- seir_generator$new()$run(t)
matplot(y_seir[, "t"], y_seir[, c("S", "E", "I", "R")],
        type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("steelblue", "orange", "firebrick", "darkgreen"),
        xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Number of people")
legend("right", legend = c("S", "E", "I", "R"), lwd = 2, bty = "n",
       col = c("steelblue", "orange", "firebrick", "darkgreen"))
```

## SEIR vs SIR

Compared with the SIR from lecture 1, the same $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$ now
gives a later, broader peak — the latent period slows the epidemic down even
though it does not change $R_0$. Rather than take that on trust, plot both:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
sir_generator <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I
  deriv(I) <- beta * S * I - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N0    <- user(1000)
  I0    <- user(1)
  beta  <- user(2e-4)
  gamma <- user(0.1)
})
y_sir <- sir_generator$new()$run(t)
plot(t, y_sir[, "I"], type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "grey60",
     xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Infectious (I)")
lines(t, y_seir[, "I"], lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", legend = c("SIR", "SEIR (4-day latent period)"),
       col = c("grey60", "firebrick"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

Same total transmission, spread over a longer time: later, lower peak.

## Births and deaths: demography

So far the epidemic is a one-off: everyone ends up in $R$ and nothing else
happens.

Over longer horizons, births replenish the susceptible pool. Add a
per-capita birth/death rate $\mu$:

- births enter $S$
- deaths leave every compartment at rate $\mu$
- $N$ stays constant
- we now need $N = S + E + I + R$ explicitly for the birth term

We use fast turnover (mean 2 years in the population — think nursery or
boarding school) so the long-term behaviour shows on a short horizon.

## Demography in odin

```{r}
seir_demo <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- mu * N - beta * S * I - mu * S
  deriv(E) <- beta * S * I - sigma * E - mu * E
  deriv(I) <- sigma * E - gamma * I - mu * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I - mu * R
  N <- S + E + I + R
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(E) <- 0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N0    <- user(1000)
  I0    <- user(1)
  beta  <- user(2e-4)
  gamma <- user(0.1)
  sigma <- user(0.25)
  mu    <- user(1 / (2 * 365))  # mean 2 years in the population
})
```

## Endemic equilibrium

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
t_long <- seq(0, 365 * 20, by = 7)   # 20 years, weekly output
y_demo <- seir_demo$new()$run(t_long)
plot(y_demo[, "t"] / 365, y_demo[, "I"], type = "l", lwd = 2,
     col = "firebrick", xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Infectious (I)",
     xlim = c(0, 10))
```

Instead of dying out after one wave, incidence oscillates with shrinking
amplitude and settles to an endemic equilibrium — newborn susceptibles keep
transmission going.

## Time-varying parameters with `interpolate` {.scrollable}

Parameters do not have to be constant — transmission often varies over the
year, for example. odin can drive a parameter from a user-supplied time
series with `interpolate()`.

In the closed models so far, a single wave infects most of the population
and then transmission is over — there is nothing left for seasonality to
act on. To see recurrent seasonal waves we let immunity wane: recovered
people return to the susceptible compartment at rate $\omega$ (mean
immunity duration $1/\omega$, here 90 days). This is the SIRS model, with
a seasonal `beta`:

```{r}
sirs_seasonal <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I + omega * R
  deriv(I) <- beta * S * I - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I - omega * R
  beta <- interpolate(tt, bb, "linear")
  tt[] <- user()   # time points
  bb[] <- user()   # beta at each time point
  dim(tt) <- user()
  dim(bb) <- user()
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N0    <- user(1000)
  I0    <- user(1)
  gamma <- user(0.1)    # infectious period 10 days
  omega <- user(1 / 90) # immunity lasts 90 days on average
})
```

## The forcing series

Monthly values over five years, peaking in "winter":

```{r}
t_years <- 5
tt <- seq(0, 365 * t_years, by = 365 / 12)   # monthly knots
bb <- 2e-4 * (1 + 0.3 * cos(2 * pi * tt / 365))
```

Always plot the series you feed into a model, before running anything.

## The forcing series, plotted

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot(tt / 365, bb, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
     xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = expression(beta))
```

## Seasonal waves

Then pass the vectors at `$new()`; odin infers their lengths:

```{r}
m <- sirs_seasonal$new(tt = tt, bb = bb)
t_run <- seq(0, 365 * t_years, by = 1)
y_seas <- m$run(t_run)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
plot(t_run / 365, y_seas[, "I"], type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = "firebrick",
     xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Infectious (I)")
```

After the first (largest) wave, incidence settles into annual waves that
track the forcing, each peaking shortly after `beta` peaks.

## What `interpolate()` is doing

- The solver evaluates the equations at whatever times its internal steps
  require — not just at your monthly knots
- `interpolate(tt, bb, type)` turns your points into a continuous
  `beta(t)`; `type` decides what happens *between* the knots
- `dim(tt) <- user()` cannot be left out: odin compiles the model before it
  sees any data, so every array needs a declared size at compile time —
  "user" means the length is fixed at `$new()`, where odin infers it from
  the vectors you pass

## The three interpolation types

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
tt_yr <- seq(0, 365, by = 365 / 12)
bb_yr <- 2e-4 * (1 + 0.3 * cos(2 * pi * tt_yr / 365))
grid  <- seq(0, 365, by = 1)
plot(grid, spline(tt_yr, bb_yr, xout = grid)$y, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     col = "steelblue", xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = expression(beta))
lines(grid, approx(tt_yr, bb_yr, xout = grid, method = "linear")$y,
      lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
lines(grid, approx(tt_yr, bb_yr, xout = grid, method = "constant")$y,
      lwd = 2, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)
points(tt_yr, bb_yr, pch = 16)
legend("bottomleft",
       legend = c("spline (smooth)", "linear (straight segments)",
                  "constant (steps)", "knots"),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick", "darkgreen", "black"),
       lwd = c(2, 2, 2, NA), lty = c(1, 1, 2, NA),
       pch = c(NA, NA, NA, 16), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

- `"constant"` — steps; for quantities that change in jumps
- `"linear"` — joins the dots; good default for smooth drivers
- `"spline"` — smooth curve; can overshoot between widely spaced knots

## Exercise 2.1 — A less variable latent period

A single $E$ compartment implies an exponential latent period: many people
become infectious almost immediately, a few only after a very long time.

- Chain two exposed compartments $E_1 \to E_2$, each progressing at rate
  `2 * sigma`
- The mean latent period stays `1/sigma`, but is less variable (an Erlang
  distribution)

Build this model, run it with `sigma = 1/8` next to the single-$E$
version, and compare the epidemic curves.

## Exercise 2.2 — Disease-induced mortality

Extend the demography model (`seir_demo`) so that infectious people die at an
additional rate `delta` (disease-induced mortality):

- Deaths accumulate in a new compartment `D` (`deriv(D) <- delta * I`)
- The living population is no longer constant

Run 20 years with `delta = 0` and `delta = 0.01`, and plot the total
population size over time (compute it in R with `rowSums` on the compartment
columns), with the y-axis starting at 0. What happens? And what goes wrong if
you let R choose the axis limits?

## Recap

- New compartments = new `deriv()` + `initial()` lines, and re-routing
  flows
- Births and deaths turn a single epidemic into endemic dynamics
- One generator, many `$new()` calls: the scenario workflow
- Time-varying parameters: `interpolate()` drives a parameter from a
  user-supplied time series — plot the series first, then let odin infer
  the array lengths
